transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, honestly, I came in because I’m just tired all the time. And I don't mean just a little worn out from a long week, I mean... it's this heavy, constant exhaustion that I just can't seem to shake, no matter what I do. 

I work as a claims adjuster, and I've been doing it a long while, so I know the drill. It's a lot of paperwork, a lot of details. But lately, by midmorning at work, I am just completely spent. I mean, just the other day, after just reviewing a few standard files—nothing overly complicated, just the usual claims—or, you know, walking one of the junior adjusters through a claim... which I usually don't mind doing, because they really do need the help and the system can be confusing at first, but lately it just takes absolutely everything out of me. 

It feels like my body and my brain are already running on empty by 10:30 in the morning. And then I sit there looking at my computer screen, thinking about the rest of the day, all the appraisals and examiner reports I still have to double-check, and I just don't know how I'm going to get through it because the tank is just completely dry, you know? It's just this draining, heavy fatigue that makes every single little task feel like I'm trying to move through wet cement, and I just can't keep pushing through my days feeling this drained before lunch even hits.
Have you noticed a loss of interest or motivation in activities that you used to enjoy, or in things you do every day?

Well, I wouldn't say I've lost interest, really. It's more like... I just don't have the energy for them. Like my garden, for instance. I love my garden. I've been tending to those same rose bushes for, gosh, almost fifteen years now. I know exactly when to prune them, what kind of fertilizer they like, how to check for aphids—the whole nine yards. Usually, come spring, I'm out there every single weekend, getting my hands dirty, weeding the beds, making sure the soil is just right. It's always been my little sanctuary, you know? A place to just unwind after dealing with insurance claims all week. 

But lately... I still care about the roses. I still want them to bloom and look beautiful. I look out the kitchen window while I'm making my coffee in the morning, and I see the weeds starting to creep up around the base of the bushes, and I think to myself, "I really need to get out there and pull those." I have the desire to do it. I haven't lost that. But then I think about actually putting on my gardening gloves, getting down on my knees, and doing the physical work... and I just can't. The thought of the effort it takes is just so overwhelming. It's not that I don't care anymore, it's just that the fatigue is so heavy, like I was saying before, that even the things I want to do feel like climbing a mountain. So, no, the interest is still there, I promise you that. It's just... the tank is too empty to actually do any of it.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, even if it's just a subtle sense of sadness or emptiness?

Well, you know, I was actually just thinking about this the other day because my husband, Tom, he's been so wonderful through all of this. He really has. The other evening, he came home from work and he had picked up all the ingredients to make my favorite lasagna—the one with the homemade ricotta and the sweet Italian sausage that I usually only make for holidays because it's such a production. He had it all laid out on the counter, and he had even poured me a glass of that red wine I like, just trying to do something nice, you know? Just trying to cheer me up. And we had the kids over, well, they're grown now, but they came over for dinner, and it should have been this really lovely, warm evening. 

But honestly, Doctor, even sitting there with my family, with Tom being so kind and putting in all that effort... I just felt this sort of... distance from it all. It’s like, most days, I feel like there’s this gray film over everything. It’s not necessarily that I’m sitting around crying all day—though I do have my moments—but it’s more this constant, heavy dullness. Like I’m looking at my life through a dirty window. I can see that everyone is laughing and having a good time, and I know I should be happy, but the feeling just doesn’t reach me. I can go through the motions, I can smile and pass the garlic bread and ask my daughter about her new job, but I’m not really feeling the enjoyment I used to. It’s just this flat, empty feeling that sits right in my chest, pretty much all day, every day. It’s been like that for a long time now, this subtle, lingering sadness that just won't lift, no matter how good things are supposed to be.
When did these feelings of fatigue and emotional dullness first start? Have they been present continuously for the past two weeks or longer?

Well, two weeks? Oh, goodness, no. If it had only been two weeks, I don't think I would have even made an appointment. I probably would have just thought I caught a bug or needed a long weekend to catch up on my sleep. No, this... this has been going on for a lot longer than two weeks. 

It’s actually been, let me think... it’s been about three years and three months now. I know the timeline pretty exactly because it started right around the time things changed at the office. They moved me into this higher-responsibility role—which, you know, at the time I thought was a good thing. I was going to be mentoring the junior adjusters, like I mentioned before, and they also put me in charge of overseeing the implementation of these new workflow systems we were adopting. It was supposed to streamline the whole claims process, make everything more efficient. And they said, "Oh, you have so much experience, you're the perfect person to guide the team through this transition." 

And I was flattered, I really was. But almost immediately after I took on that new role, this... heaviness just started creeping in. At first, I just thought it was the stress of learning the new software while also trying to teach it to people who were still struggling with the basics of insurance adjusting. I’d come home and tell Tom, "I just need to get through this quarter, and then things will settle down." But the quarter ended, and the new system was in place, and the junior adjusters were getting the hang of it, and... I just never bounced back. The fatigue didn't lift. That gray feeling didn't go away. It’s just been this constant companion ever since that promotion, day in and day out, for over three years now. It’s like a switch flipped when I took on those new responsibilities, and I just haven't been able to flip it back, no matter how settled the job has become since then.
